title: Silver Plume Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Silver Plume wells have a 60-foot median depth, but fractured bedrock and mine history require careful site review.
h1: Silver Plume Well Depth, Yield, and Drilling Costs
intro_html:
Silver Plume sits in steep mountain terrain where most permitted wells are completed in unnamed fractured bedrock. The local records show relatively shallow wells on average, but the range is wide enough that a nearby well is not a guarantee for your lot.

Within five miles of Silver Plume, Colorado DWR records include 356 permitted wells. Only 195 report a total depth, 40 report a pump yield, and 16 report a static water level, so these figures are useful for planning but not a substitute for a site-specific drilling and water-supply review.

sections.heading: Silver Plume well depth depends on the mountain rock
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Silver Plume is 60 feet. The middle half runs from 29 to 118 feet, while the 90th percentile is 194 feet. That spread matters when you request a drilling bid: a shallow local median does not eliminate the possibility of drilling substantially deeper on a particular parcel.

Seventy percent of reported wells are under 100 feet, 24% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 4% between 300 and 600 feet, and 2% exceed 600 feet. The deepest record is 802 feet. Permits identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers for 326 wells, with only 2 identifying fractured granite and 9 identifying alluvial water. Fractured granite and gneiss can change quickly across short distances.

sections.heading: Reported yields are generally workable, but records are limited
sections.html:
Among the 40 wells that report a pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 8.8 to 13.2 gallons per minute. Seventy-five percent of those reported yields are between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 20% are above 15 gallons per minute. No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute, while 5% are between 1 and 5 gallons per minute.

That is a favorable record for ordinary household planning, but the sample is small compared with the 356 permitted wells. A yield test and storage-tank plan still matter, especially for a full-time home, multiple fixtures, livestock, or a property with a slow-recovering fractured-rock well. Colorado exempt household-use wells also have a 35 gallon-per-minute pumping limit.

sections.heading: Water levels are shallow in the available Silver Plume records
sections.html:
Only 16 wells report a static water level. Their median depth to water is 20 feet, with the middle half from 8 to 41 feet. That suggests water is commonly encountered relatively close to the surface in the reported wells, but it does not tell you the static level on an untested parcel.

The permit-by-decade series describes permitting activity, not groundwater levels: records show 1 permit in the 1950s, 6 in the 1960s, 32 in the 1970s, 42 in the 1980s, 67 in the 1990s, 63 in the 2000s, 43 in the 2010s, and 21 in the 2020s. It therefore does not demonstrate that the water table is dropping. Ask for a measured static level and recovery information from any existing well.

sections.heading: Silver Plume permits span decades, with several active drillers
sections.html:
The oldest permit in this local record dates to the 1950s, and the newest was issued in 2025. Domestic and household wells make up 61% of the use mix. Monitoring wells account for 25%, while stock wells account for 4% and irrigation wells 2%. The records also include many older permits, so confirm that a well on a property was actually constructed, properly permitted, and approved for its intended use.

The most frequent driller names in the records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 26 wells, followed by Mcpherson Drilling Company (Mcpherson, Benny Don) and James Drilling (Keaton, Jordan K.), with 12 each. These are permit-record names, not a recommendation. A driller should review access, casing and grout requirements, the proposed well location, and the water right before work begins.

sections.heading: What a new well can cost around Silver Plume
sections.html:
Local drilling conditions are fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. The stated drilling rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 60-foot median depth, the drilled hole models to about $3,900 to $6,000.

A finished system with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $9,900 to $18,000 at that median depth. A deeper hole can move outside that range, and the total may also change with difficult access, casing and grout needs, rock conditions, and the distance from the well to the building. Get a written bid that separates drilling from the pump, storage, electrical, trenching, and any required road or site work.

sections.heading: Mine history and mountain conditions deserve a careful check
sections.html:
The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 5 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1,276 historic mine features, and 14 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped features do not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but they are strong reasons to review environmental records and test water rather than relying only on appearance or taste.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible in fractured bedrock even where nearby wells perform well. Before buying, inspect the well construction, pump test, static water level, water-quality results, and any treatment equipment. Also confirm septic setbacks, usable building area, and access for a drill rig. A good water source does not solve a lot that cannot support a permitted septic system or practical construction access.

sections.heading: Use nearby wells to plan, not to promise, your result
sections.html:
Start with the DWR permit records for Silver Plume and compare them with wells in Georgetown, Empire, Downieville-Lawson-Dumont, St. Mary's, Montezuma, and Idaho Springs. The closest useful comparison is usually a nearby well with similar geology, construction date, depth, and intended use—not simply the closest point on a map.

For a vacant lot, confirm the water-right position and the type of permit available before choosing a house plan. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required. For an existing home, have the well and pump inspected, collect a current water sample, and verify that the recorded well matches the equipment and location on the ground. Price the full system and site work before treating the property as build-ready.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Silver Plume?
faq.a: The median reported depth is 60 feet, and the middle half of reported wells runs from 29 to 118 feet. Seventy percent are under 100 feet, but the deepest record reaches 802 feet. Because Silver Plume wells commonly use fractured bedrock, neighboring depths can vary sharply. Use nearby permits for planning, then have a driller evaluate the specific lot.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Silver Plume?
faq.a: The local drilling model is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 60-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $3,900 to $6,000. A finished system with a pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $9,900 to $18,000. Access, casing, grout, rock conditions, and a deeper-than-median hole can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Silver Plume wells produce?
faq.a: Among 40 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 8.8 to 13.2 gallons per minute. Seventy-five percent of reported yields fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. The sample is limited, so request a yield test and recovery information before relying on a well for a home.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Silver Plume?
faq.a: Safety depends on the individual well and test results. Within about 10 miles, records map 5 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1,276 historic mine features, and 14 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These locations do not establish contamination at your property. Test existing or new well water and review nearby environmental records, especially where mining or cleanup features are close.

faq.q: Are Silver Plume wells at risk of running dry?
faq.a: The available records do not prove a declining water table. Only 16 wells report static water levels, with a median depth to water of 20 feet and a middle half from 8 to 41 feet. Fractured mountain bedrock can produce uneven results, including low-yield or dry holes. Review nearby well depths, yields, recovery, and construction before buying or building.
